To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chlordiazepoxides, a benzodiazepene derivative, inhibits the binding of [3H](3MeHis2)TRH to its binding site, but only at a relatively high concentration (IC50 of 5 micro M in brain tissue and 290 nM pituitary tissue).
chlordiazepoxde displaces [3H](3MeHis2)TRH from its receptor site in a noncompetitive manner in brain tissue and in a competitive manner in pituitary gland tissue.
chlordiazepoide displaces [3H](3MeHis2)TRH binding and the inhibition produced is apparently noncompetitive in the brain but is competitive in the pituitary.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new drugs that are useful in the treatment of anxiety, insomnia, epilepsy and other disorders of the central nervous system.
the development of an assay for the measurement of the TRH receptor complex.
the interaction of the benzodiazepinergic system with the TRH receptor complex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chlordiazepoxides do bind to the TRH receptor complex and this interaction is apparently different between brain and pituitaries.
chlordiazepoxides are capable of displacing [3H](3MeHis2)TRH from its receptor site and that this effect is not mediated via the classical benzodiazapine receptor.
chlordiazepoxides are not classical benzodiazapine agonists but that they do have some affinity for a TRH receptor complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chlordiazepoxides, but not all benzodiazepenes, displace TRH binding.
chlordiazepoxides are not classical ligands for the benzodiazepinic site but may be useful for the study of the TRH receptor complex.
chlordiazepoxides are not the only benzodiazepinoid compounds to bind to the TRH receptor, and the benzodiazepinoic compounds may be a class of compounds that bind to the TRHR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the benzodiazepinone chlordiazepoxid (CDP) binds to and inhibits the binding of the peptide hormone TRH to its receptors.
chlordiazepoxides are able to inhibit TRH binding to its receptor, but only at relatively high concentrations.
the benzodiazepinergic system is more complex than we previously thought.
